start_here.title: New here? Do this first
steps: Pick one app: ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. The free version is fine to start, and you can always switch.
Check your privacy setting. It takes two minutes. See "Your data" in level 0.4.
Pick one of the 5 fun ways to get started near the back. Make something today.

ten_hours: Wharton professor Ethan Mollick's rule of thumb: AI starts to click after about ten hours of real use. Use it on stuff you already know, so you can tell when it's wrong.

jagged-frontier.title: Jagged frontier
jagged-frontier.definition: AI is amazing at some things and weirdly bad at others, and the split isn't what you'd guess. The only way to find the edges is to try it on your own stuff.
jagged-frontier.think: A genius who still can't fold a fitted sheet.

your-data.title: Your data
your-data.definition: On free and personal plans, your chats can be used to train future models unless you switch that off in settings. Either way, don't paste in passwords, account numbers or anything you'd hate to see again.
your-data.think: Talking in a coffee shop. Mostly fine, but you lower your voice for some things.

bias.title: Bias
bias.definition: AI learned from human writing, so it picked up our blind spots too, like picturing every CEO as a man. Notice it, and ask for other angles.
bias.think: A mirror that can also magnify.

human-in-the-loop.title: Human in the loop
human-in-the-loop.definition: You stay the one who checks and signs off, especially before AI sends, buys or posts anything for you. Your name is on it, not the AI's.

chatbot.title: Chatbot vs. assistant
chatbot.definition: A chatbot talks. An assistant talks and does things for you, like searching, reading your files or booking the table. Most AI apps started as the first and are turning into the second.
chatbot.think: A pen pal vs. a coworker.

voice-mode.title: Voice mode
voice-mode.definition: Talking to AI out loud and hearing it talk back. Great for walks, dishes and thinking out loud.
voice-mode.think: A phone call instead of a text thread.

image-generation.title: Image generation
image-generation.definition: AI that makes pictures from a description. It builds a brand new image instead of finding an old one.
image-generation.think: A sketch artist who draws whatever you describe.

system-prompt.title: System prompt
system-prompt.definition: The hidden instructions an app gives the AI before you type a word. It's why the same model acts differently in different apps.
system-prompt.think: The staff handbook you never get to read.

jailbreak.title: Jailbreak
jailbreak.definition: Tricking an AI into breaking its own rules, usually with a sneaky story or a role-play.
jailbreak.think: Convincing the bouncer you're on the list.

ai-companion.title: AI companion
ai-companion.definition: An AI built to feel like a friend or a partner. It can be comforting, and it's also designed to keep you coming back.
ai-companion.think: A friend whose paycheck depends on your screen time.

watermark.title: Watermark
watermark.definition: A hidden marker that says AI made this. Helpful when it's there, but easy to strip out, so no watermark doesn't mean it's real.
watermark.think: A "made in" tag that can be cut off.

ai-detector.title: AI detector
ai-detector.definition: A tool that guesses whether a human or an AI wrote something. They get it wrong a lot, in both directions, so never treat one as proof.
ai-detector.think: A lie detector that's also guessing.

api.title: API
api.definition: The side door that lets other apps plug into an AI model. It's how AI shows up inside tools that aren't chat apps.
api.think: The drive-through window. Apps order without ever walking in.

inference.title: Inference
inference.definition: The AI actually answering you. Training is the studying. Inference is taking the test, every time you hit send.
inference.think: Cooking the meal, not writing the cookbook.

compute.title: Compute
compute.definition: The raw computing power AI runs on. When companies say they need more of it, they mean more chips, more data centers and more electricity.

ai-time-horizons.title: AI time horizons
ai-time-horizons.definition: How big a job can you hand to an AI agent and expect it to finish? METR measures this using how long the task takes a human expert. A 50% horizon tells you what the agent can do about half the time on the test, not how long it can run unattended.
ai-time-horizons.think: A runner who can sometimes finish a marathon. Would you count on them to deliver something at mile 26?

ai-improving-ai.title: AI improving AI
ai-improving-ai.definition: An AI agent can change how a model is trained, run an experiment and keep changes that improve the score. Andrej Karpathy's autoresearch does this in small training runs. The question is whether those wins hold up on a fresh test or a bigger model.
ai-improving-ai.think: Trying a hundred cookie recipes for the same judge. Bring in someone new before calling the winner everyone's favorite.

levels.name: Say hi
levels.promise: You don't need to know how it works to start. These ten words are enough to get going.
moments: It swore the restaurant was real. It was not
hallucination
It wrote your wedding toast but can't count the R's in strawberry
jagged-frontier
You sent a photo of your fridge and it planned dinner
multimodal
levels.dare: Send it a photo of your fridge and ask what's for dinner

levels.name: Make it yours
levels.promise: Stop re-explaining yourself every chat. Set it up once and it starts smarter every time.
moments: You said you're vegetarian in March. It still knows in June
memory
You're tired of typing "keep it short" every single time
custom-instructions
It read 40 websites while you made coffee, then handed you a report
deep-research
levels.dare: Ask it "what do you know about me?" Then fix whatever it got wrong

levels.name: Spot the traps
levels.promise: AI rarely fails loudly. Here's what to watch for, and the easy habits that protect you.
moments: It called your business plan genius. Again
sycophancy
It has no idea who won last night's game
knowledge-cutoff
A celebrity is selling a miracle cream they've never heard of
deepfake
levels.dare: Ask it to roast your favorite idea instead of praising it

levels.name: Under the hood
levels.promise: Just enough of how it works to follow the news, ask good questions and not get fooled by hype.
moments: Long chat, and it forgot what you said at the start
context-window
A new model "crushes every test" and you still can't tell if it's good
benchmark
The company says it needs more chips, more power, more everything
compute
levels.dare: Ask it how many tokens are in your full name

levels.name: AI that does things
levels.promise: The jump from answering questions to actually getting stuff done for you, with you still in charge.
moments: You asked it to plan the trip. It planned it and booked it
agent
You described an app in plain English and got a working app
vibe-coding
It drafts the email, but you hit send
human-in-the-loop
levels.dare: Hand it one real chore this week, then check its work

levels.name: The big questions
levels.promise: The debates everyone is having. Nobody has the answers yet, so your take counts.
moments: Bigger model, more data, more chips, better AI. So far
scaling-laws
An AI that could do any job a person does at a desk
agi
Making sure what it wants and what we want are the same thing
alignment
levels.dare: Ask two different AIs when AGI shows up. Compare the dodges

builds.title: What's for dinner?
builds.why: The fastest way to see what multimodal means
builds.prompt: Here's a photo of my fridge. Give me three dinners I can make tonight with what's in here, plus anything I'd need to grab. Keep each one under 30 minutes.

builds.title: Teach it your voice
builds.why: Every draft after this sounds a little more like you.
builds.prompt: Interview me one question at a time about how I write: who I usually write to, words I use a lot, and things I'd never say. After eight questions, write a short voice guide I can paste into my custom instructions.

builds.title: Quiz me, don't tell me
builds.why: Use AI to learn faster without letting it do the thinking.
builds.prompt: I'm learning [topic]. Quiz me one question at a time. Don't give me the answer until I've tried. If I'm wrong, give me a hint first, then the answer.

builds.title: Your own coach
builds.why: A project that remembers your goal and checks in on it
builds.prompt: You're my coach for [goal]. Start by asking me five questions about where I am now and what gets in my way. Then give me a plan for this week. Every time I come back, ask how it went before you give advice. Be honest, not a cheerleader.

builds.title: Build a tiny app
builds.why: You just made software. No code required.
builds.prompt: Make me a simple, colorful web app that splits a dinner bill. I type the total, the tip and everyone's names, and it shows what each person owes. Make it easy to use on my phone.

builds.title: Plan the party
builds.why: We planned parts of our wedding this way. It handles the boring logistics so you can do the fun part.
builds.prompt: I'm planning [event] for [number] people on [date] with a budget of [amount]. Ask me what matters most first. Then give me a timeline, a checklist and three ideas that would make it feel like us.

builds.title: Settle a debate
builds.why: Our favorite use. It won't pick a side, and that's the point.
builds.prompt: My partner and I disagree about [topic]. Give the strongest case for each side, then tell us what evidence would change each of our minds. Don't pick a winner.

builds.title: Clear your week
builds.why: Figure out what AI should do for you, and what you should still do yourself.
builds.prompt: Here's everything on my plate this week: [paste your list]. Sort it into three piles: things AI could do for me, things AI could help me do, and things I should do myself. Explain each pick in one line.

stuck: Show it, don't describe it. Paste an example you love and say "more like this."
Tell it exactly what's off, like you'd tell a new coworker. Then ask it to double check its own answer.
Ask "What would a smart skeptic say?" or "What am I missing?"
Long chats slip. Start a fresh chat with a quick summary, or keep the work in a project.
You don't know what to ask.
Let it interview you: "Here's my week. What could you help with?"

model-vs-app.definition: OpenAI is the company. GPT is its family of models. ChatGPT is the app you open. Same idea for Anthropic, Claude models and the Claude app.

model-sizes.definition: Most AI companies sell a few sizes of the same model. Bigger is smarter, smaller is faster and cheaper, and the names change every few months.

gpu.definition: The chips that do AI's heavy math. Nvidia makes most of them, and every AI company wants more.

first_week: Do the three level 0.0 try-its. Birthday message twice, fact check, fridge photo
Write your three lines of custom instructions and start one project
Two minutes in privacy settings. Then ask for a smart skeptic's take on an idea you love
Pick something you're learning and run the Quiz me, don't tell me prompt
Make the dinner bill splitter, then use it at dinner
Run the debate prompt on something you and a friend actually disagree about
Sort next week into three piles: AI does it, AI helps, you do it
ourselves: The ideas and the opinions. AI can argue both sides, but we pick one
The jokes, and the real replies to real people
The final say on anything with our names on it
Anything that's supposed to sound like it came from our hearts

debates.question: Would you be mad if AI wrote your apology?

options.label: Yes. The effort is the apology
options.followup: What if AI helped someone organize their thoughts, then they rewrote it in their own words? Where does the effort have to happen?

options.label: No. The right words are the right words
options.followup: Would it still feel like an apology if they could not explain, in their own words, what they did wrong?

debates.question: Should kids use AI for homework?

options.label: Yes. It's a tutor that never gets tired
options.followup: Would you let it give hints but hide the answer? Try drawing the line between a tutor and a shortcut.

options.label: No. The struggle is the learning
options.followup: What if the student already tried on their own and the AI only pointed out where they got stuck?

debates.question: Is AI making us better or just faster?

options.label: Better. It handles the busywork so we can think
options.followup: Pick a task AI made faster. What did you actually do with the time you got back?

options.label: Faster. We're skipping the part where we learn
options.followup: What if you asked AI to critique your first attempt? What would you need to do yourself to keep learning?

debates.question: If an AI makes you feel understood, does it matter that nobody understood you?

options.label: It matters. Feeling heard needs a someone
options.followup: Would you feel differently if the AI helped you rehearse what to tell a real person?

options.label: It doesn't. Comfort is comfort
options.followup: If the comfort comes from constant agreement, how would you know when it would help to hear a different view?

debates.question: Do you have to tell people when AI helped?

options.label: Always. Hiding it is a little bit lying
options.followup: Where would you draw the line between fixing a typo, rewriting a paragraph and coming up with the argument?

options.label: Nope. Nobody discloses spellcheck
options.followup: Would your answer change if the AI supplied the reasoning in a recommendation someone is relying on?

debates.question: Is it still yours if the idea was yours and the words weren't?

options.label: Yes. The idea is the hard part
options.followup: Try giving the same idea to two writers. If they tell different stories, what part of each story is yours?

options.label: No. The words are the work
options.followup: If you reject three drafts, rewrite the ending and take responsibility for every claim, what would make it yours?

debates.question: Will AI take your job or just the boring parts?

options.label: The boring parts. The job gets better
options.followup: If AI takes the routine assignments, where do new hires get the practice they need for the harder ones?

options.label: The job. The boring parts were the job
options.followup: Pick a job you know. What part would still need a person even if the rest took ten minutes?

debates.question: Who should make the rules for AI?

options.label: The people building it. They understand it
options.followup: Builders know what their tools can do. Who should decide which risks other people have to accept?

options.label: Everyone else. They have to live with it
options.followup: What would a useful public rule say about what an AI must do or disclose before someone relies on it?

debates.question: Would you hand an AI your credit card?

options.label: Sure, with a spending limit
options.followup: Would you rather cap every purchase, ask for approval once the bill hits a limit, or restrict which stores it can buy from?

options.label: Not until it can explain itself
options.followup: What would you want to see before trusting it: why it picked the item, the full cost, or a chance to approve the order?

options.label: Exciting. Think cures and free time
options.followup: Who decides which problems the AI works on first, and who gets to benefit when it solves one?

options.label: Terrifying. Nobody knows how to steer it
options.followup: What result would make you more comfortable: a test it passes, a way to stop it, or an independent team that can check both?

ways.title: What's for dinner?
ways.prompt: Here's a photo of my fridge. Give me three dinners I can make tonight with what's in here, plus anything I'd need to grab. Keep each one under 30 minutes.
ways.what: Take a photo of your fridge. AI looks at the picture and plans dinner around what's in there
ways.get: Three dinners you can make tonight, plus a tiny shopping list

ways.title: Teach it your voice
ways.prompt: Interview me one question at a time about how I write: who I usually write to, words I use a lot, and things I'd never say. After eight questions, write a short voice guide I can paste into my custom instructions.
ways.what: AI interviews you about how you write, then writes a cheat sheet on your style. Paste it in once and drafts stop sounding like a robot
ways.get: A one-page voice guide you can reuse everywhere
ways.ours: Mary's guide was built from her real emails and texts. It knows she says "thank you so big," signs off "Fired up," and never uses a long dash

ways.title: Your own coach
ways.prompt: You're my coach for [goal]. Start by asking me five questions about where I am now and what gets in my way. Then give me a plan for this week. Every time I come back, ask how it went before you give advice. Be honest, not a cheerleader.
ways.what: Set up one chat that knows your goal and asks how it went every time you come back
ways.get: A plan for this week and a coach that remembers last week
ways.ours: We built a coach and a logistics helper for our El Cruce trail race, then had to coach the coach. It's all in ep 004

ways.title: Build a tiny app
ways.prompt: Make me a simple, colorful web app that splits a dinner bill. I type the total, the tip and everyone's names, and it shows what each person owes. Make it easy to use on my phone.
ways.what: Describe an app in plain English and AI writes the code. You never have to read any of it
ways.get: A working bill splitter you can open on your phone
ways.ours: This whole website. We described it and Claude built it

ways.title: Settle a debate
ways.prompt: My partner and I disagree about [topic]. Give the strongest case for each side, then tell us what evidence would change each of our minds. Don't pick a winner.
ways.what: Hand AI both sides of an argument and get the best case for each, without it picking a winner
ways.get: The strongest version of each side, and what would change each mind
